rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The created eyes, tongue, lips, and guidance to two paths demonstrate God's power against the disbeliever's claim that no one can overpower him.
rows.anchor: ألم نجعل له عينين * ولسانا وشفتين * وهديناه النجدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Najd means an elevated road; clear proofs resemble it because they are evident to minds as a high road is to sight.
rows.anchor: قال أهل العربية : النجد الطريق في ارتفاع

rows.speaker: عامة المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes understand the two paths as the paths of good and evil.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا التأويل ذهب عامة المفسرين في النجدين

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet saying the two paths are good and evil, and one should not prefer evil's path to good's.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي هريرة أنه عليه السلام قال : إنما هما النجدان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This guidance recalls the passage saying humanity was guided to a path and may be grateful or ungrateful.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية كالآية في : { هل أتى على الإنسان }

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says the boaster asks who will account for the wealth he claims to have spent; the answer is the One who created his limbs.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن : قال : { أهلكت مالا لبدا }

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وسعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib identify the two paths as the breasts, routes to an infant's life and provision; God guides the infant to suckle.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس وسعيد بن المسيب ، أنهما الثديان

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal prefers the good-and-evil interpretation and argues that the creator of a rational heart and articulate tongue can destroy what He made and knows what creatures conceal.
rows.anchor: قال القفال : والتأويل هو الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Manifest gifts leave no excuse for disbelief or for using God-given wealth to taunt God and the supporters of His religion.
rows.anchor: فما العذر في الذهاب عن هذا مع وضوحه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God points to virtuous uses of wealth and identifies the disbeliever's spending as wasteful and ineffective.
rows.anchor: دل عباده على الوجوه الفاضلة التي تنفق فيها الأموال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iqtihām means entering a difficult matter; an ʿaqaba is a steep mountain path, plural ʿaqab or ʿiqāb.
rows.anchor: الاقتحام الدخول في الأمر الشديد يقال : قحم يقحم قحوما

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAta interprets the obstacle as a ravine of Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء : يريد عقبة جهنم

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the obstacle is a barrier between Paradise and Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي : هي عقبة بين الجنة والنار

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Umar identifies the obstacle as a slippery mountain in Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عمرهي : جبل زلال في جهنم

rows.speaker: مجاهد والضحاك
rows.claim: Mujahid and al-Dahhak identify it as the bridge over Hell, matching al-Kalbi's barrier interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد والضحاك : هي الصراط يضرب على جهنم

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi objects that people have not crossed Hell's obstacle, making that interpretation obvious; the following verse explains it as freeing a slave and feeding someone.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي : وهذا تفسير فيه نظر

rows.speaker: الحسن ومقاتل
rows.claim: Hasan and Muqatil understand the obstacle as a metaphor for struggling against the self and Satan in virtuous acts.
rows.anchor: وهو قول الحسن ومقاتل : قال الحسن عقبة الله شديدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi prefers the moral-struggle reading: rising from sense and imagination to divine lights involves lofty and arduous obstacles.
rows.anchor: وأقول هذا التفسير هو الحق

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says the negative is repeated in meaning: failing to cross means neither freeing a slave nor feeding someone.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : إنها متكررة في المعنى

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abu Ali al-Farisi reads lā as lam, so repetition is unnecessary; repetition elsewhere is like repeating lam.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي الفارسي : معنى { فلا اقتحم العقبة }

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal reads the line as a rebuke: why did he not spend his wealth on what entails crossing the obstacle?
rows.anchor: قال القفال : قوله : { فلا اقتحم العقبة } أي هلا أنفق ماله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpreters keep the apparent past-tense sense: he did not cross the obstacle.
rows.anchor: وأما الباقون فإنهم أجروا اللفظ على ظاهره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse omits 'crossing': an obstacle cannot literally be slave emancipation, and the ellipsis magnifies religious commitment.
rows.anchor: فلا بد من تقدير محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fakk is release from a restrictive bond; freeing a neck removes the legal status of slavery, like releasing a fetter or pledge.
rows.anchor: الفك فرق يزيل المنع كفك القيد والغل

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says the verbal noun is fakāk, with fatḥa on the fāʾ, not kasra.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : في المصادر فكها يفكها فكاكا بفتح الفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabs bound captives by neck and hands, so releasing a captive came to be called fakkāk even without actual shackles.
rows.anchor: ويقال : كانت عادة العرب في الأسارى شد رقابهم

rows.speaker: الأخطل
rows.claim: Al-Akhtal's verse uses breaking shackles as evidence for the expression.
rows.anchor: قال الأخطل : أبني كليب إن عمي اللذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Freeing a neck can mean manumitting a slave or helping a contracted slave pay for freedom.
rows.anchor: فك الرقبة قد يكون بأن يعتق الرجل رقبة

rows.speaker: البراء بن عازب
rows.claim: Al-Bara ibn ʿAzib reports a Bedouin asking the Prophet for an act leading to Paradise; the Prophet distinguishes direct manumission from helping fund another's release.
rows.anchor: روى البراء بن عازب ، قال : ( جاء أعرابي إلى رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is freeing one's own soul through worship that leads to Paradise and release from the Fire.
rows.anchor: وفيه وجه آخر وهو أن يكون المراد أن يفك المرء رقبة نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading has the nouns 'freeing a neck or feeding'; another has the verbs 'free a neck or feed' as a substitute for 'crossed the obstacle.'
rows.anchor: قرىء : ( فك رقبة ) أو إطعام

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra prefers the verbal reading because the following 'then he was' is a verb coordinated with 'freed/fed'; a nominal reading would fit if the text said 'then indeed he was.'
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : وهو أشبه الوجهين بصحيح العربية

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says dhā maqraba means a person of kin; calling someone 'my kinship' is awkward because qarāba is a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : ذا قرابة تقول زيد ذو قرابتي

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says the orphan is related to the giver, combining orphanhood and kinship claims and making feeding especially meritorious.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل : يعني يتيما بينه وبينه قرابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kinship may also mean nearness through neighborhood, as well as lineage.
rows.anchor: وقيل : يدخل فيه القرب بالجوار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage recalls the people of the right described in al-Waqiʿa among thornless lote trees and clustered fruit.
rows.anchor: وإنما ذكر ذلك لأنه تعالى بين حالهم في سورة الواقعة

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf explains right and left as directions or auspiciousness and ill omen: people blessed or ill-starred for themselves.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) : الميمنة والمشأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The left-side people may be those who receive their record in the left hand or from behind their backs.
rows.anchor: فقيل : المراد من يؤتي كتابه بشماله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their earlier description includes scorching wind, boiling water, and shade of black smoke.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم وصف الله لهم بأنهم : { فى سموم وحميم

rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج والمبرد
rows.claim: Al-Farra, al-Zajjaj, and al-Mubarrad say both āṣada and awṣada mean to close a door.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء والزجاج والمبرد : يقال آصدت الباب وأوصدته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With hamza, the reading may derive from āṣada or from awṣada with hamz of wāw after a ḍamma.
rows.anchor: فمن قرأ مؤصدة بالهمزة أخذها من آصدت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without hamza, it may follow the unhamzed awṣada form or ease the hamza in āṣada to wāw, as in other words.
rows.anchor: ومن لم يهمز احتمل أيضا أمرين

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra notes that aṣīd and waṣīd mean a tightly closed door.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : ويقال من هذا الأصيد والوصيد

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says Hell's doors remain shut forever: no door opens, grief leaves, or relief enters.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل { عليهم نار مؤصدة } يعني أبوابها مطبقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the flames surround them, as in al-Kahf's image of Hell's enclosure.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد إحاطة النيران بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word can describe a fire with shut doors; omitting the genitive construction restores tanwīn because the two forms alternate.
rows.anchor: المسألة الثانية : { * المؤصدة } هي الأبواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi accepts the concern that an infinitival mā disrupts the sequence and the Qadi's concern about delaying an oath by the sky's Creator; he answers that the order stages sense before reason.
rows.anchor: والذي يخطر ببالي في الجواب عنه : أن أعظم المحسوسات هو الشمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the sun's four attributes, God is described through three acts over the sky, earth, and composite beings, represented by the soul; this guides reason from sensible creation to divine majesty.
rows.anchor: ثم ذكر ذاته المقدسة بعد ذلك ووصفها بصفات ثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky's construction signals that the sun and celestial bodies are originated: their finite, chosen sizes require a measurer and planner.
rows.anchor: وذلك لأن الشمس والسماء متناهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The builder analogy shows that the planner sized the sun and heavens by choice, establishing their origination.
rows.anchor: وكما أن باني البيت يبنيه بحسب مشيئته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using mā instead of man can describe the mighty agent who built the sky; mā can also mean man, but Razi relies on the first explanation.
rows.anchor: الأول : أن المراد هو الإشارة إلى الوصفية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's three signs cover the physical world: simple bodies include upper heaven and lower earth, while the noblest composites are ensouled beings; the unseen is inferred from the visible.
rows.anchor: لأن الاستدلال على الغائب لا يمكن إلا بالشاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth follows the sky because another verse says that God spread the earth after that.
rows.anchor: إنما أخر هذا عن قوله : { والسماء وما بناها }

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says ṭaḥw is like daḥw, meaning spreading; exchanging ṭāʾ for dāl is permitted, so the earth was expanded.
rows.anchor: قال الليث : الطحو كالدحوا وهو البسط

rows.speaker: عطاء والكلبي
rows.claim: ʿAta and al-Kalbi say God spread the earth over water.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء والكلبي : بسطها على الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If nafs means the body, its proportioning is the balanced arrangement of its organs; if it means the governing faculty, God gave it hearing, sight, imagination, thought, and memory.
rows.anchor: إن حملنا النفس على الجسد ، فتسويتها تعديل أعضائها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading of the indefinite 'a soul' is the unique sacred prophetic soul, chief among composites, animals, humans, and prophets.
rows.anchor: أن يريد به نفسا خاصة من بين النفوس ، وهي النفس القدسية النبوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively it means every soul; the indefinite signals multiplicity, since every animal species has a distinct soul and properties beyond human comprehension.
rows.anchor: أن يريد كل نفس ، ويكون المراد من التنكير التكثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation says God made the soul understand good and evil, know one as good and the other as bad, and choose; this matches Muʿtazili doctrine and is attributed to Ibn Abbas and senior exegetes.
rows.anchor: أن إلهام الفجور والتقوى ، إفهامها وإعقالهما

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr glosses God's inspiration as imposing wickedness and piety on the soul.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير : ألزمها فجورها وتقواها

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says God put this in the soul by granting success to piety or abandoning it to wickedness.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد : جعل فيها ذلك بتوفيقه إياها للتقوى

rows.speaker: الزجاج والواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj and al-Wahidi prefer the second interpretation: inspiration differs from teaching or explanation and means God places something in the heart, committing the person to it.
rows.anchor: واختار الزجاج والواحدي ذلك

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi derives inspiration from a root meaning to swallow or take in, then its use for what God casts into the heart; Ibn Zayd's reading best fits that origin.
rows.anchor: وأصل معنى الإلهام من قولهم : لهم الشيء ، والتهمه إذا ابتلعه

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير وعطاء وعكرمة ومقاتل والكلبي
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿAta, ʿIkrima, Muqatil, and al-Kalbi interpret the successful soul as one God purified and enabled to obey.
rows.anchor: المروي عن سعيد بن جبير وعطاء وعكرمة ومقاتل والكلبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi rejects the Muʿtazili reading: after showing God directs the cosmos, the verse says even voluntary acts fall under His decree.
rows.anchor: فههنا لم يبق شيء مما في عالم المحسوسات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Choices cannot arise without a maker, since that makes a created event uncaused; if the servant makes them, regress follows, so their cause is God.
rows.anchor: فحصولها إن كان لا عن فاعل فقد استغنى المحدث عن الفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi appeals to experience: an image may suddenly enter an inattentive mind, produce desire, then bodily movement, showing inspiration as divine enabling or abandonment.
rows.anchor: فإنه ربما كان الإنسان غافلا عن شيء فتقع صورته في قلبه دفعة

none: Verse quotation and transition to its explanation only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tazkiya means purification or growth; one reading says a person succeeds by purifying the soul through obedience and avoiding sin.
rows.anchor: فاعلم أن التزكية عبارة عن التطهير أو عن الإنماء

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: The Qadi accepts the alternative that God purifies the soul by judging or naming it pure, while saying the self-purifying reading is closer because nafs is the explicit antecedent.
rows.anchor: وقبل القاضي هذا التأويل ، وقال المراد منه أن الله حكم بتزكيتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi rejects the naming interpretation: verbal forms indicate bringing about, and an unchangeable divine judgment cannot change from truth to falsehood or knowledge to ignorance.
rows.anchor: لأن بناء التفعيلات على التكوين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi argues that the nearest antecedent is 'inspired it,' closer to mā than 'a soul,' so grammar supports his interpretation.
rows.anchor: فإن أهل اللغة اتفقوا على أن عود الضمير إلى الأقرب

rows.speaker: سعيد بن أبي هلال
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi reports from Saʿid ibn Abi Hilal that the Prophet paused at this verse and prayed for his soul's piety and purification, naming God as its guardian.
rows.anchor: ما رواه الواحدي في البسيط عن سعيد بن أبي هلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dassa is derived from tad sīs, concealing one thing in another; the original d-s-s form was altered by replacing one sīn with yāʾ.
rows.anchor: فقالوا : { دساها } أصله دسسها من التدسيس

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila say the righteous show themselves openly while sinners hide; generous Arabs publicize camps and night fires, unlike misers hiding from people seeking aid.
rows.anchor: أن أهل الصلاح يظهرون أنفسهم ، وأهل الفسق يخفون أنفسهم

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: A second Muʿtazili gloss is that the loser concealed himself among the righteous despite not belonging to them.
rows.anchor: خاب من دساها } أي دس نفسه في جملة الصالحين

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: Another gloss says the loser buried himself in sins until submerged in them.
rows.anchor: من دساها } في المعاصي حتى انغمس فيها

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: Another says a person instills wickedness through persistent sin and keeping sinful company.
rows.anchor: من دس في نفسه الفجور ، وذلك بسبب مواظبته عليها

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: A final gloss says abandoning obedience for sin leaves a person obscure and forgotten, like a thing hidden away.
rows.anchor: أن من أعرض عن الطاعات واشتغل بالمعاصي صار خاملا

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Razi's school says a soul fails when God misguides, seduces, makes it wicked, invalidates, and destroys it.
rows.anchor: وأما أصحابنا فقالوا : المعنى خابت وخسرت نفس أضلها الله تعالى

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi says God swears by the noblest creatures to the success of the soul He purifies and the loss of the one He abandons, precluding self-directed purification or ruin outside prior decree.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي رحمه الله : فكأنه سبحانه أقسم بأشرف مخلوقاته

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says ṭughyān and ṭugwā are verbal nouns; ṭugwā fits the verse endings, like daʿwā from daʿā.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : الطغيان والطغوى مصدران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common interpretation is that Thamud's rebelliousness drove them to deny the messenger.
rows.anchor: أنها فعلت التكذيب بطغيانها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes ṭugwā as the punishment they denied when they disbelieved the messenger's warning.
rows.anchor: أن الطغوى اسم لعذابهم الذي أهلكوا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says the punishment reading is plausible because ṭughyān means exceeding bounds; the unusual cry could be called ṭugwā, as al-Hāqqa names their punishment with related terms.
rows.anchor: لأن معنى الطغيان في اللغة مجاوزة القدر المعتاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inbaʿatha is the reflexive of baʿatha, as when someone is sent to act and goes forth; here the most wretched rose to hamstring the she-camel.
rows.anchor: انبعث مطاوع بعث يقال : بعثت فلانا على الأمر فانبعث له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view identifies the worst man as the camel-killer Qudar ibn Salif, proverbial for ill fortune and called the worst of earlier people by the Prophet.
rows.anchor: أنه شخص معين واسمه قدار بن سالف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another takes the phrase collectively: an elative can remain singular with a plural or dual noun, as in 'these two are the best people.'
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكونوا جماعة ، وإنما جاء على لفظ الوحدان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messenger is Salih; he warned them that God's she-camel was a sign of divine unity and his prophethood, forbidding harm and interference with her water.
rows.anchor: المراد من الرسول صالح عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She and their livestock had alternating drinking days, which harmed their herds; Salih had repeatedly warned of punishment, so his brief warning sufficed.
rows.anchor: كان لها شرب يوم ولهم ولمواشيهم شرب يوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāqat Allāh is an accusative warning construction, elliptically meaning 'leave her alone and beware her watering'; do not withhold it or take it exclusively.
rows.anchor: ناقة الله } نصب على التحذير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning of punishment did not prevent Thamud from denying Salih or hamstringing the she-camel.
rows.anchor: لم يمتنعوا عن تكذيب صالح ، وعن عقر الناقة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: The act can be attributed to one direct perpetrator, Qudar, or to the whole people for approving it; Qatada reports that everyone pledged before the deed, as most exegetes say.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة : ذكر لنا أنه أبى أن يعقرها حتى بايعه صغيرهم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says the camel's killers were two men.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء : قيل إنهما كانا إثنين

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says damdama means covering them with punishment, enveloping them from every side.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : معنى دمدم أطبق عليهم العذاب

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi connects damdama with staining or coating something with fat, yielding punishment smeared all around them.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي : الدم في اللغة اللطخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading of damdama is burying or leveling them beneath the earth.
rows.anchor: تقول للشيء : يدفن دمدمت عليه

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari says damdama means anger or disturbing speech.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري : دمدم غضب

rows.speaker: ثعلب عن ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Thaʿlab transmits from Ibn al-Aʿrabi that damdama means shaking the earth over them; al-Farra adopts this view.
rows.anchor: رواه ثعلب عن ابن الأعرابي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If damdama means enveloping punishment, 'made it even' means Gabriel's cry killed everyone alike; if it means leveling, God flattened the earth over them.
rows.anchor: وذلك أن هلاكهم كان بصيحة جبريل عليه السلام

none: Verse quotation and transition to its explanation only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view takes the unstated subject as God, the nearest referent; He does not fear consequences because His acts are just and wise.
rows.anchor: أنه كناية عن الرب تعالى إذ هو أقرب المذكورات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A related explanation treats the phrase as belittling the deed, too insignificant to fear consequences, though God is exalted beyond such fear.
rows.anchor: ذكر ذلك لا على وجه التحقيق لكن على وجه التحقير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation stresses extreme punishment: unlike a king who fears consequences and restrains himself, God feared no outcome and held nothing back.
rows.anchor: فإن كل ملك يخشى عاقبة ، فإنه يتقي بعض الاتقاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second referent is Salih, who does not fear the aftermath of their punishment, promising his protection from harm.
rows.anchor: أنه كناية عن صالح الذي هو الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third referent is Thamud's most wretched man, who did not fear the consequences of hamstringing the she-camel; the delayed verse is read earlier in meaning.
rows.anchor: المراد أن ذلك الأشقى الذي هو أحيمر ثمود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says nine camel-killers plotted to murder Salih, were stoned by angels, then sought him after their faces yellowed; he fled to a pagan protector and the punishment overtook them.
rows.anchor: روي أن صالحا لما وعدهم العذاب بعد ثلاث ، قال التسعة الذين عقروا الناقة

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal says the sura was revealed about Abu Bakr's spending on Muslims and Umayya ibn Khalaf's miserliness and disbelief, while its message applies generally.
rows.anchor: قال القفال رحمه الله : نزلت هذه السورة في أبي بكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its general scope is evident from statements that human striving differs and that the audience is warned of a blazing Fire.
rows.anchor: إلا أنها وإن كانت كذلك لكن معانيها عامة للناس

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali reports that the Prophet said every soul's destination is known to God; when companions asked whether to rely on that, he told them to act, since each person is facilitated toward what they were created for.
rows.anchor: ويروى عن علي عليه السلام أنه قال : ( خرجنا مع رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath may invoke the powerful creator who made male and female from one fluid, or Adam and Eve, God's act of creating them, or the one who created them with mā meaning man.
rows.anchor: أي والقادر العظيم القدرة الذي قدر على خلق الذكر والأنثى من ماء واحد

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to have recited 'by the male and the female,' omitting the relative phrase.
rows.anchor: قرأ النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم { والذكر * والأنثى }

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud's reading is 'by the One who created the male and the female.'
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود : ( والذي خلق الذكر والأنثى )

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi reads the words in genitive, taking them as what God created, with male and female in apposition; God's name is implicit because only He creates.
rows.anchor: وعن الكسائي : { وما خلق الذكر والأنثى } بالجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Swearing by male and female covers all living creatures; even an intersex person must be classed as male or female for a divorce-oath ruling.
rows.anchor: القسم بالذكر والأنثى يتناول القسم بجميع ذوي الأرواح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wisdom required God to explain worship, distinguish obedience from sin, offer guidance and exhortation, and call people to worship for their benefit, mercy, and lasting bliss.
rows.anchor: أخبرهم أنه قد قضى ما عليه من البيان والدلالة

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila argue that God excuses people and only commands what they can do, so He does not impose the impossible.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى أباح الأعذار وما كلف المكلف إلا ما في وسعه

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: They argue that 'upon Us' means a duty is incumbent upon God, and that guidance would be pointless if humans did not originate actions independently.
rows.anchor: أن كلمة على للوجوب ، فتدل على أنه قد يجب للعبد

rows.speaker: الواحدي عن الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi transmits al-Farra's reading 'guidance and misguidance,' with misguidance elided as in 'garments protect from heat,' which also implies cold; Ibn Abbas via ʿAta says God guides allies to obedience and bars enemies from it.
rows.anchor: وذكر الواحدي وجها آخر نقله عن الفراء فقال المعنى : إن علينا للهدى والإضلال

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila reject that reading by citing the distinction that the straight path is God's charge but the crooked path is not from Him.
rows.anchor: قالت المعتزلة : هذا التأويل ساقط لقوله تعالى : { وعلى الله قصد السبيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading says both abodes belong to God, so human guidance does not affect His dominion; compelling people away from sin would nullify moral responsibility, so He guides through explanation, promises, and warnings.
rows.anchor: أن لنا كل ما في الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading says God owns both abodes and grants them to whom He wills, so people should seek both kinds of happiness from Him.
rows.anchor: أن لنا ملك الدارين نعطي ما نشاء من نشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says the first interpretation better suits the Muʿtazila and the second his own school.
rows.anchor: والأول أوفق لقول المعتزلة ، والثاني أوفق لقولنا

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: The Qadi objects that other sinners would be excluded from Hell; Razi replies that every disbeliever denied the prophet and turned away from examining his signs, so all disbelievers fit the description.
rows.anchor: أن كل كافر لا بد وأن يكون مكذبا للنبي في دعواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that the verse encourages sin fails: present-world blame and God's withholding honor and reward can deter, and punishment may take other forms.
rows.anchor: يكفي في الزجر عن المعصية حصول الذم في العاجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inference that everyone less than the most pious enters Hell relies on a converse implication the Qadi rejects; it would wrongly send children and the insane there.
rows.anchor: والتمسك بدليل الخطاب وهو ينكر ذلك فكيف تمسك به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qadi's claim that the warning names only a particular blazing fire is weak, since the phrase can describe all Hell; another verse calls it a blaze that strips the skin.
rows.anchor: لأن قوله : { نارا تلظى } يحتمل أن يكون ذلك صفة لكل النيران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading 'most wretched' as merely more deserving of Hell abandons the apparent meaning without evidence.
rows.anchor: لأنه ترك للظاهر من غير دليل

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi says yaṣlāhā means enduring the Fire's heat: unbelievers remain there, whereas a sinful believer either never enters or later escapes.
rows.anchor: ما ذكره الواحدي وهو أن معنى : { لا يصلاها }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the general wording can be qualified by verses warning sinful believers of punishment.
rows.anchor: أن يخص عموم هذا الظاهر بالآيات الدالة على وعيد الفساق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sayujannab means He will distance or set someone apart from the Fire.
rows.anchor: معنى سيجنبها أي سيبعدها ويجعل منها على جانب

rows.speaker: أجمع المفسرون منا
rows.claim: Razi says Sunni exegetes unanimously identify the most pious person as Abu Bakr; Shia reject this and identify Ali, citing the verse about giving alms while bowing.
rows.anchor: أجمع المفسرون منا على أن المراد منه أبو بكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi argues the most pious is the best of creation: 49:13 makes the most God-fearing most honored; piety is observable and superiority is not, so the known quality identifies the unknown rank.
rows.anchor: إن المراد من هذا الأتقى هو أفضل الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse cannot mean Ali, Razi argues, because the Prophet raised, fed, clothed, and cared for Ali, creating a worldly favor to repay; prophetic guidance is not repayable.
rows.anchor: لأنه كان في تربية النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the community agrees its best member after the Prophet was either Abu Bakr or Ali, and the description excludes Ali, Razi concludes it identifies Abu Bakr.
rows.anchor: لأن الأمة مجمعة على أن أفضل الخلق بعد رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Bilal, enslaved by ʿAbd Allah ibn Judʿan, was sold to polytheists with camels after complaints about his treatment of idols; they tortured him in the heat as he repeated 'One, One.'
rows.anchor: كان بلال ( عبدا ) لعبد الله بن جدعان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet told Bilal God would save him, then informed Abu Bakr of the torture; Abu Bakr bought him with gold, and the claim that Bilal owed him a favor prompted the verse.
rows.anchor: ثم أخبر رسول الله أبا بكر أن بلالا يعذب في الله

rows.speaker: ابن الزبير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr says Abu Bakr bought and freed weak slaves; when his father urged him to buy protection for himself, Abu Bakr said he sought to protect his own back, and the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الزبير وهو على المنبر : كان أبو بكر يشتري الضعفة من العبيد

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf says yat azakkā may be an appositive of 'gives,' with no syntactic case inside the relative clause, or a circumstantial accusative modifying the subject of 'gives.'
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) في محل : { يتزكى } وجهان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parse treats seeking the Lord's face as an exception unlike the preceding favor: he owes nobody a favor and only seeks God's face.
rows.anchor: ابتغاء وجه ربه } مستثنى من غير جنسه وهو النعمة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra supplies an implied verb of spending: he spends only to seek his Lord's face, as in 2:272.
rows.anchor: وذكر الفراء فيه وجها آخر وهو أن يضمر الإنفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pious giver is not repaying an earlier gift or favor, which would merely settle a debt; reward is due because he gives in response to God's command.
rows.anchor: لا يؤتيه مكافأة على هدية أو نعمة سالفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anthropomorphists appeal to 'face' and deniers to 'his highest Lord' as implying another lord; Razi says these issues were discussed earlier.
rows.anchor: المجسمة تمسكوا بلفظة الوجه والملحدة تمسكوا بلفظة

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو بكر الباقلاني
rows.claim: Al-Baqillani contrasts Ali's feeding verse, motivated by God's face and fear of Judgment, with Abu Bakr's verse, which he reads as pure devotion without hope of reward or fear of punishment; he ranks Abu Bakr higher.
rows.anchor: ذكر القاضي أبو بكر الباقلاني في كتاب الإمامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say seeking God means seeking His reward and honor because seeking His essence is impossible; others affirm love of God Himself, a question discussed at 2:165.
rows.anchor: من الناس من قال : ابتغاء الله بمعنى ابتغاء ذاته وهي محال

rows.speaker: يحيى بن وثاب
rows.claim: Yahya ibn Waththab reads seeking the Lord's face in the nominative, supported by a dialect that raises an exception, as in the cited poem.
rows.anchor: قرأ يحيى بن وثاب : { إلا ابتغاء وجه ربه } بالرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading promises Abu Bakr contentment in the afterlife through his reward.
rows.anchor: فالمعنى أنه وعد أبا بكر أن يرضيه في الآخرة بثوابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi prefers the greater alternative: Abu Bakr gave seeking God's approval and God will be pleased with him; divine pleasure in a servant surpasses the servant's pleasure in God, and both are promised as in 89:28.
rows.anchor: وفيه عندي وجه آخر ، وهو أن المراد أنه ما أنفق إلا لطلب رضوان الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cessation of revelation need not mean removal from prophethood; it could signal that the mission is complete and death near, which is good because the Prophet's afterlife portion is better.
rows.anchor: انقطاع الوحي لا يجوز أن يكون لأنه عزل عن النبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because 'your Lord has not abandoned you' conferred great honor, the next verse assures the Prophet that his afterlife portion with God will be greater still.
rows.anchor: لما نزل : { ما ودعك ربك } ( الضحى : 3 ) حصل له بهذا تشريف عظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi also suggests future conditions will surpass past ones, with God increasing the Prophet's honor and rank day by day.
rows.anchor: ما يخطر / ببالي ، وهو أن يكون المعنى وللأحوال الآتية خير لك من الماضية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The afterlife is better because God there does what He wills, whereas the Prophet can do what he wants in worldly life.
rows.anchor: كأنه تعالى يقول له إنك في الدنيا على خير لأنك تفعل فيها ما تريد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His nation will join him in Paradise like children joining a father; the Qur'an calls his wives believers' mothers and his descendants a delight of the eyes.
rows.anchor: الآخرة خير لك يجتمع عندك أمتك إذ الأمة له كالأولاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The afterlife is his possession while this world is not; even if it were lesser, what he owns is better than what he does not, and in reality it is far superior.
rows.anchor: الآخرة خير لك لأنك اشتريتها ، أما هذه ليست لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this world disbelievers taunt him, but in the next his nation witnesses over other nations and he over prophets, with God testifying for him.
rows.anchor: في الدنيا الكفار يطعنون فيك أما في الآخرة فأجعل أمتك شهداء على الأمم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly delights are few, tainted, and fleeting, whereas afterlife delights are many, pure, and everlasting.
rows.anchor: أن خيرات الدنيا قليلة مشوبة منقطعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise says 'for you' rather than 'for you all' because some companions' afterlife may be worse; universalizing it would be false, while naming only the obedient exposes sinners and hypocrites.
rows.anchor: لأنه كان في جماعته من كانت الآخرة شرا له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses said his Lord was with him and would guide him, while Muhammad said God was with 'us,' since only a prophet and the certainly blessed Abu Bakr accompanied him.
rows.anchor: ولهذا السبب قال موسى عليه السلام : { كلا إن معى ربى سيهدين }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Moses led thousands in three days of rain supplication, withheld because a backbiter was among them; after God revealed that man had died, Moses found seventy biers at the prayer ground.
rows.anchor: وروي أن موسى عليه السلام خرج للاستسقاء ، ومعه الألوف ثلاثة أيام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The saying about crouched elders hints at this community's special favor: God rejected thousands because of one sinner but pardons sinners because of one obedient person.
rows.anchor: عليه السلام قال : ( لولا شيوخ ركع ) وفيه إشارة إلى زيادة فضيلة هذه الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise is singular because the Prophet is its central recipient and believers follow him; honoring his companions honors him because he rejoices more in their reward than his own.
rows.anchor: أنه المقصود وهم أتباع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other prophets say 'myself' to receive their reward before their nations, while Muhammad says 'my nation' because he longs to see them rewarded.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك حيث تقول الأنبياء : نفسي نفسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When struck by opponents, the Prophet prayed for their guidance, but when the trench kept him from prayer he prayed against them; he accepted bodily injury, not injury to religion, so God exalted him.
rows.anchor: حين شجوا وجهك ، قلت : ( اللهم اهد قومي فإنهم لا يعلمون )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says God does not declare someone an unbeliever merely for years of missed prayer or preventing another's prayer, but does for harming even a hair or part of the Prophet's sandal.
rows.anchor: فقلت من ترك الصلاة سنين ، أو حبس غيره عن الصلاة سنين لا أكفره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using 'soon' means the Prophet's death is not near and he will live longer.
rows.anchor: أنه يدل على أنه ما قرب أجله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future promise answers the polytheists' claim that Muhammad would soon die, echoing God's earlier denial that He had abandoned or hated him.
rows.anchor: ثم قال المشركون : سوف يموت محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says Gabriel speaks the whole sura to the Prophet because he longed intensely for him and his speech, and God wanted Gabriel to give the good news.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة من أولها إلى آخرها كلام جبريل عليه السلام معه

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf calls the lām before sawfa emphatic lām of initiation; it cannot be an oath-lām without emphatic nūn, so an omitted subject is understood: 'You will surely be given.'
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) : هي لام الابتداء المؤكدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired emphasis and delay mean the gift is certain even if it comes later for a wise reason.
rows.anchor: معناه : أن العطاء كائن لا محالة ، وإن تأخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next verse specifies the extent of the afterlife's superiority: God's gift reaches the limit of what the Messenger desires and approves.
rows.anchor: فبين بهذه الآية مقدار ذلك التفاوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the afterlife is better because God grants everything the Prophet wants, beyond what worldly life can contain.
rows.anchor: لأنه يعطيه كل ما يريده وذلك مما لا تتسع الدنيا له

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the gift includes a thousand palaces of white pearl in Paradise, with musk for soil.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس : ألف قصر في الجنة من لؤلؤ أبيض

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب وابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ali and Ibn Abbas identifies the gift as intercession for the community; the Prophet said he would not be satisfied while any follower remained in the Fire.
rows.anchor: فالمروى عن علي بن أبي طالب عليه السلام وابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says intercession is the necessary reading: God commanded the Prophet to seek forgiveness for believers, and promising what pleases him entails granting that request for sinners.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن الحمل على الشفاعة متعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding assurance fits intercession: God will not abandon or hate the Prophet, and will spare his companions, followers, and devotees from anger to please him and soothe his heart.
rows.anchor: كأنه تعالى يقول لا أودعك ولا أبغضك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Numerous intercession reports show the Prophet is pleased when sinners are forgiven; combined with the promise to fulfill his pleasure, they establish intercession.
rows.anchor: الأحاديث الكثيرة الواردة في الشفاعة دالة على أن رضا الرسول

rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق
rows.claim: Jaʿfar al-Sadiq says his grandfather's satisfaction is that no monotheist enters the Fire.
rows.anchor: وعن جعفر الصادق عليه السلام أنه قال : رضاء جدي

rows.speaker: الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Baqir says the People of the House call this the most hopeful verse: it is intercession for monotheists until the Prophet says he is satisfied; others cite 39:53.
rows.anchor: وعن الباقر ، أهل القرآن يقولون : أرجى آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A worldly reading includes victories at Badr and Mecca, mass conversions, victory and expulsion of Jewish tribes, campaigns across Arabia, the caliphs' conquests, fallen empires, captured treasuries, and Islam's spread.
rows.anchor: فهو إشارة إلى ما أعطاه الله تعالى من الظفر بأعدائه يوم بدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi prefers to include blessings of both this world and the next.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن الأولى حمل الآية على خيرات الدنيا والآخرة

none: Verse text only; no commentary in this segment.
